Efficiency improvement​ - Transform personal experience and project requirements into reusable rules, allowing a single configuration to remain effective over time, reducing communication costs with AI and manual review time.​ - Standardization​ - Structure team guidelines and project standards into rules so that the content managed by all members remains consistent in style, structure, and quality, avoiding deviations.​ - Quality assurance​ - Ensure that AI understands the project's core constraints (such as architecture design, naming conventions, code style, and more), preventing common errors.​ Types of rules​ You can configure two types of rules: user rules and project rules.​ ​ | | | | --- | --- | | Rule Type​ | Description​ | | Global rules​ | Global rules are rules customized for the AI based on personal usage habits and needs, aiming to make the AI's output better meet the user's personalized requirements. Global rules take effect in all projects.​
The following are example use cases:​
- Language style: Preference for concise, rigorous, humorous, or other styles of expression.​
- Operating system: Provide answers specific to Windows or macOS operating systems.​
- Content depth: Whether detailed explanations, examples, or only conclusions are needed.​
- Interaction mode: For example, whether to prefer direct answers or guided questions.​ | | Project rules​ | Project rules are the rules that the AI must follow for the current project, and they are only effective within the current project.​
The following are example use cases:​
- Code style: Indentation (spaces/tabs), naming conventions (camelCase/snake\_case), and more.​
- Language and framework: Preferred programming languages (such as Python/JavaScript) or frameworks (such as React/Django).​
- API restrictions: Do not use certain APIs.​ | ​ Create global rules​ Create one or more global rules according to your personal preferences. The AI will comply with the global rules you create in all projects.​ 1. In IDE mode, click the Settings icon in the upper-right corner to enter the settings center.​ - OR​ - In SOLO mode, click the Settings icon in the upper-right corner of the chat panel to enter the settings center.​ 2. In the left navigation panel, select Rules.​ - The rule management panel appears.​ 3. In the Rules section, click the \+ Create button, and select Global from the drop-down list.​ 4. In the rule input box, enter a global rule, then click the ​Save button.​ - ​ ​​![]()​ ​ - The global rule you add will be displayed in the rule list.​ Create project rules​ Procedure​ Project rules are written using Markdown syntax and are only effective within the project in which they are created.​ When creating project rules, you can specify how the rules take effect. Depending on the application mode, the system will automatically modify the rule's alwaysApply property. You also need to configure the rule's description or globs property according to the activation method.​ The steps for creating project rules are as follows:​ 1. Open a project.​ 2. In IDE mode, click the Settings icon in the upper-right corner to enter the settings center.​ - OR​ - In SOLO mode, click the Settings icon in the upper-right corner of the chat panel to enter the settings center.​ 3. In the left navigation panel, select Rules.​ - The rule management panel appears.​ 4. In the Rules section, click the \+ Create button, and select Project from the drop-down list. ​ 5. In the Create Rule popup, enter the rule name, then click the ​Confirm button.​ - The system will automatically create a .trae/rules folder in the project's directory, create the rule file you named in that folder, and open the rule file in the editor for editing.​ - ​ ​​![]()​ ​ 6. Set the rule's ​Application Mode.​ - ​ | | | | --- | --- | | Application Mode​ | Description​ | | ​Always Apply​ | This rule is effective for all AI chats within the current project.​ | | ​Apply to Specific Files​ | This rule is only effective when matching files specified in the globs field. When the file you mention in the chat input box matches the globs setting, this rule will be automatically activated.​ | | ​Apply Intelligently​ | Based on the use case you add for this rule in the description field, the AI will determine relevance in the chat and decide whether to use this rule.​ | | ​Apply Manually​ | This rule is only effective when it is mentioned in a chat using #Rule.​ | ​ 7. Set relevant properties in the form according to the rule's application mode.​ - ​ | | | | --- | --- | | Application Mode​ | Property Settings​ | | ​Always Apply​ | The alwaysApply field has been automatically set to true.​ | | ​Apply to Specific Files​ | - The alwaysApply field has been automatically set to false.​
- At ​File Pattern, use wildcards to specify the files to which the rule applies (for example, \*.js, src/\*\*/\*.ts), and you can configure multiple wildcards separated by ,. This setting will be automatically synchronized to the globs field.​ | | ​Apply Intelligently​ | - The alwaysApply field has been automatically set to false.​
- At ​Description, enter the use case for this rule, for example: When writing test code for React components, use this rule. This setting will be automatically synchronized to the description field.​ | | ​Apply Manually​ | The alwaysApply field below has been automatically set to false.​ | ​ 8. Below \-\-\-, add the rule's content using Markdown syntax.​ 9. Click the ​Save button.​ About multi-level rule nesting​ When there are many rules in the project root directory, placing all types of rules directly in the .trae/rules/ root directory makes searching and maintenance difficult.​ You can create subfolders under the .trae/rules/ directory and categorize rule files of the same type into the corresponding subfolders. The system will automatically read the rules in these directories recursively. Currently, up to three levels of nesting are supported.​ The structure is as follows:​ ​ Plain Text Copy .trae/rules/ ​ ├── global-rules.md ​ ├── module-a/ # Level 1​ │ ├── rules-a.md​ │ ├── submodule-a1/ # Level 2​ │ │ └── rules-a1.md​ │ └── submodule-a2/ # Level 2​ │ └── submodule-a2-b1/ # Level 3​ │ ├── rules-a2-b1.md ← Deepest readable level​ │ └── submodule-a2-b1-c1/ # Level 4 (unreadable）​ │ └── rule-a2-b1-c1.md ← Exceeds limit (unreadable）​ └── module-b/ # Level 1​ └── rules-b.md​ ​ About creating rules for subdirectories​ In a large project, there are usually multiple folders, each representing a different module or technology stack. If all rules (including AGENTS.md) are configured in the project root directory, it is not only difficult to maintain but may also cause exclusive rules for one module to interfere with other modules.​ TRAE supports reading the .trae/rules/ folder in any subdirectory of the project. To configure rules for a specific module, you can directly place the rule files in that module's folder. When you mention files in that directory in a chat, or when the AI reads files in that directory while dealing with tasks, the system will automatically apply the exclusive rules in that directory.​ Example structure:​ ​ Plain Text Copy my-project/​ ├── .trae/​ │ └── rules/ # Project root directory​ │ └── global-style.md​ ├── frontend-module/ # A frontend module​ │ ├── AGENTS.md # Takes effect only when files related to frontend-module are read or mentioned​ │ └── .trae/​ │ └── rules/ # Takes effect only when files related to frontend-module are read or mentioned​ │ └── react-best-practices.md​ └── backend-module/ # A backend module​ └── .trae/​ └── rules/ # Takes effect only when files related to backend-module are read or mentioned​ └── api-design.md​ ​ Reference rules in a chat​ - For rules of the “​Always Apply” type, each chat will reference them by default, and they will be displayed in the upper-left corner of the chat input box.​ - ​ ​​![]()​ ​ - For rules of the “​Apply Manually” type, reference them in the chat input box using #Rule.​ - ​ ​​![]()​ ​ - Note Among rule referencing methods, #Rule has the highest priority. For project rules with application mode of “​Apply to Specific Files” or “​Apply Intelligently”, if you mention these rules in the chat using #Rule, the AI will also use them in this chat.​ ​ Edit/delete rules​ 1. In the ​Rules list in the settings center, find the target rule.​ 2. Click the Settings icon on the right.​ 3. Select ​Edit or ​Delete in the menu.​ - ​ ​​![]()​ ​ 4. Complete the corresponding operation.​ Use AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, and CLAUDE.local.md​ - AGENTS.md​ - AGENTS.md is a lightweight markdown file located in the project's root directory, used to provide behavioral guidance to AI agents. Through intuitive and easy-to-read textual descriptions, it clearly specifies the instructions and standards that agents must follow within the project. The rules defined in AGENTS.md are project-level rules and only take effect within the current project.​ - An AGENTS.md file created in TRAE can be reused in other IDEs that support AGENTS.md, and vice versa.​ - LAUDE.md & CLAUDE.local.md​ - TRAE is compatible with CLAUDE.md and CLAUDE.local.md. If you have created a project in Claude Code and added CLAUDE.md and/or CLAUDE.local.md, these files will be imported together when you import the project into TRAE.​ To enable AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, and CLAUDE.local.md as context for TRAE:​ 1. Go to Settings \> Rules.​ 2. In ​Import Settings, toggle the ​Include AGENTS.md in the context. and ​Include CLAUDE.md in context switches on.​ - Once enabled, the agent will read the CLAUDE.md and CLAUDE.local.md files in the root directory and add them to the context.​ - ​ ​​![]()​ ​ Set rules for Git commit messages​ TRAE supports setting rules for AI-generated Git commit messages to ensure they meet project requirements. You only need to configure the scene: git\_message field in the rule file.​ The scene: git\_message field is compatible with existing fields such as alwaysApply, description, and globs. As long as the rule file contains this field, regardless of how other fields are configured, the AI will follow the rule in scene: git\_message when generating Git commit messages.​ If multiple rule files in the project contain scene: git\_message, the AI will follow the rules in all of these files.​ Method 1: Add rules to an existing file​ The steps for setting rules for AI-generated Git commit messages are as follows:​ 1. In the current project, open an existing rule file.​ 2. Add the scene field to the file and set it to git\_message.​ 3. Add desired rules below the \-\-\- separator.​ - The structure is as follows:​ - ​ Markdown Copy \-\-\-​ scene: git\_message​ \-\-\-​ Body: Rules for generating Git commit messages.​ ​ Method 2: Add rules in the git-commit-message.md file​ 1. In the left navigation bar, click the Source Contro icon.​ - This opens the Source Control panel.​ 2. On the right side of the top commit message input box, click the dropdown icon, then select Configure Commit Message Generation Rules from the menu.​ - The system automatically generates the git-commit-message.md file in the .trae/rules directory.​ - Note If you have already added scene: git\_message and rules in an existing rule file, the system will open that file directly instead of creating git-commit-message.md.​ ​ - ​ ​​![]()​ ​ 3. Add desired rules in the git-commit-message.md file.​ How to let the AI generate Git commit messages？​ 1. Open the Source Control panel.​ 2. Click the Generate Commit Message icon, or click the dropdown icon and select Generate Commit Messag from the menu.​ - ​ ​​![]()​ ​ Best practices​ - Control the granularity of each rule's content to avoid including too much information in a single rule, keeping it clear, focused, and easy to understand.​ - Rules must not conflict with or override each other.​ - When specifying file paths, use relative paths based on the project root directory to ensure that the AI can accurately locate the file.​ - When referencing rules, prioritize those that are strongly related to the current chat or task.​ - After creating or modifying a rule, it is recommended to start a brand new chat before using it to avoid conflicts between historical context and the new rule.​ - If there is already a large amount of non-compliant code in the project, AI may follow the existing code style rather than the new rules. In this case, it is recommended to:​ - Clearly inform the model that the current task is “refactoring”.​ - In specific scenarios, require the AI to strictly follow the new rules.​ - Initiate a dedicated refactoring project to gradually improve the overall code quality.​ Example​ Rules for different use cases​ Basic interaction General coding Refactoring Code readability Performance optimization - All responses must be provided in Chinese.​ - If code is provided, add concise Chinese comments for key logic and sections that may be difficult to understand.​ - When the generated code exceeds 20 lines, first consider whether appropriate abstraction or aggregation can be applied.​ ​ Multi-level nesting of project rules​ Suppose your project has many rules related to frontend design and development; you can organize them as follows:​ ​ Plain Text Copy .trae/rules/​ ├── general-rules.md # General rules​ ├── frontend/​ │ ├── react-best-practices.md # React standards​ │ ├── css-naming.md # CSS naming conventions​ │ └── testing/​ │ └── unit-test-rules.md # Frontend unit test standards​ ├── backend/​ │ ├── api-design.md # API design standards​ │ └── error-handling.md #
